name: Payload Lab Export
description: Educational payload templates for security testing training

metadata.warning: EDUCATIONAL TEMPLATES ONLY - DO NOT USE FOR UNAUTHORIZED TESTING

payloads.explanation: Semicolon command separator - executes whoami after original command (Linux/Unix)
payloads.defensive_notes: Input validation: whitelist allowed characters. Never pass user input directly to system(), exec(), shell_exec(). Use argument arrays, not shell strings.

payloads.explanation: Pipe operator - passes output of first command to whoami (usually shows username)
payloads.defensive_notes: Avoid shell execution entirely. Use language-native APIs (subprocess with shell=False in Python, child_process.execFile in Node).

payloads.explanation: OR operator - executes whoami if first command fails
payloads.defensive_notes: Principle of least privilege: run application with minimal OS permissions. Disable shell access if possible.

payloads.explanation: Background execution - runs whoami in background (Linux/Unix)
payloads.defensive_notes: Use parameterized command execution. In PHP: escapeshellarg() + escapeshellcmd() as last resort, better to avoid shell.

payloads.explanation: AND operator - executes whoami only if first command succeeds
payloads.defensive_notes: Strict input validation: whitelist known-good inputs. Monitor process execution for anomalies.

payloads.explanation: Windows command separator using ampersand
payloads.defensive_notes: On Windows: use subprocess without shell=True. Avoid cmd.exe entirely. Use Windows API directly when possible.

payloads.explanation: Windows pipe operator - works in cmd.exe and PowerShell
payloads.defensive_notes: In .NET: use Process.Start() with argument lists, never with shell command strings.

payloads.explanation: Newline separator - executes as separate command in some contexts
payloads.defensive_notes: Normalize and validate input. Remove/escape control characters including newlines and carriage returns.

payloads.explanation: Backtick command substitution - output of whoami replaces the expression (Linux/Unix)
payloads.defensive_notes: Never use shell metacharacters in commands. Whitelist approach: define allowed values, reject everything else.

payloads.explanation: Dollar-parenthesis command substitution - modern syntax in bash/sh
payloads.defensive_notes: Use application-level functions instead of OS commands when possible. For file operations: use language file APIs, not cat/ls/dir.

payloads.explanation: Windows environment variable expansion - can leak sensitive paths
payloads.defensive_notes: Disable or sanitize environment variable expansion. In cmd.exe, use setlocal to limit variable scope.

payloads.explanation: Internal Field Separator variable - used to bypass space filtering in bash
payloads.defensive_notes: Blacklist filtering is insufficient. Use structured command execution (execve with argv array).

payloads.explanation: Output redirection - writes command output to file (potential for file creation/overwrite)
payloads.defensive_notes: File system permissions: ensure web user cannot write to sensitive directories. Monitor for unexpected file creation.

payloads.explanation: Input redirection - reads from file and uses as command input (potential information disclosure)
payloads.defensive_notes: Restrict read access to sensitive files. Use SELinux/AppArmor to enforce mandatory access control.

payloads.explanation: Error redirection - combines stderr with stdout (can reveal error messages with sensitive info)
payloads.defensive_notes: Don't display raw command output/errors to users. Log securely, show generic error messages to users.

payloads.explanation: Windows output redirection to file
payloads.defensive_notes: On Windows: NTFS permissions to restrict file operations. Use User Account Control (UAC) properly.

payloads.explanation: Empty string injection - bypasses simple string matching for 'whoami'
payloads.defensive_notes: Don't rely on blacklisting commands. Whitelist allowed inputs or avoid shell execution entirely.

payloads.explanation: Special variable insertion ($@ = empty in many contexts) to obfuscate command
payloads.defensive_notes: Complex bypass attempts indicate attack. Use allowlist validation + logging of rejected inputs.

payloads.explanation: Backslash escaping - can bypass pattern matching in some shells
payloads.defensive_notes: Normalize input before validation. Remove escape sequences or reject inputs containing them.

payloads.explanation: Full path + empty backticks - bypasses command name filters
payloads.defensive_notes: Whitelist acceptable values, don't blacklist commands. Better: don't use shell at all.

payloads.explanation: Brace expansion in bash - {cat,/etc/passwd} expands to 'cat /etc/passwd'
payloads.defensive_notes: Use bash with --norc --noprofile options if shell is unavoidable. Better: use execve() directly.

payloads.explanation: Windows caret escape character - 'who^ami' becomes 'whoami' in cmd.exe
payloads.defensive_notes: On Windows: avoid cmd.exe. Use ProcessStartInfo with UseShellExecute=false in .NET.

payloads.explanation: Combined obfuscation: backslash escape + IFS variable for space
payloads.defensive_notes: Multiple obfuscation layers indicate sophisticated attack. Defense: no shell execution + strict validation.

payloads.explanation: URL-encoded newline separator - may execute as separate command after decoding
payloads.defensive_notes: Decode user input, then validate. Check for encoded metacharacters. Reject, don't try to sanitize.
